title: What is TransactionTemplate and how does programmatic transaction management work? Explain execute vs executeWithoutResult, how it compares to @Transactional, and how it fixes the self-invocation problem.

s1_definition.profdef: `TransactionTemplate` is a Spring helper class that lets you manage transactions in your own code instead of relying on the `@Transactional` annotation. You wrap the code that must run inside a transaction in a callback, and the template takes care of starting the transaction before the callback runs, committing it if the callback finishes normally, and rolling it back if the callback throws a runtime exception. It wraps a `PlatformTransactionManager` and gives you fine-grained, line-by-line control over exactly which statements are inside the transaction.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the National Bank of India. With `@Transactional`, Rajesh hands his whole form to a clerk and says "do everything or nothing." With `TransactionTemplate`, Rajesh himself stands at the counter, says "open the ledger now" (begin), writes exactly the two lines he wants (debit his savings, credit Priya), and then says "close and stamp the ledger" (commit). If anything looks wrong mid-way, he tears up the page (rollback). He controls the exact start and end point of the transaction himself.
s1_definition.oneliner: `TransactionTemplate` is you driving the transaction manually — begin, run your code, commit or rollback — instead of letting the annotation drive for you.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `TransactionTemplate` is a Spring helper class that lets you manage transactions in your own code instead of relying on the `@Transactional` annotation. You wrap the code that must run inside a transaction in a callback, and the template takes care of starting the transaction before the callback runs, committing it if the callback finishes normally, and rolling it back if the callback throws a runtime exception. It wraps a `PlatformTransactionManager` and gives you fine-grained, line-by-line control over exactly which statements are inside the transaction.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the National Bank of India. With `@Transactional`, Rajesh hands his whole form to a clerk and says "do everything or nothing." With `TransactionTemplate`, Rajesh himself stands at the counter, says "open the ledger now" (begin), writes exactly the two lines he wants (debit his savings, credit Priya), and then says "close and stamp the ledger" (commit). If anything looks wrong mid-way, he tears up the page (rollback). He controls the exact start and end point of the transaction himself.

**One line to remember:** `TransactionTemplate` is you driving the transaction manually — begin, run your code, commit or rollback — instead of letting the annotation drive for you.

sections.s2_technical:
A `TransactionTemplate` is created from a `PlatformTransactionManager`. In Spring Boot the transaction manager is auto-configured, so you just inject it and build the template once: `new TransactionTemplate(txManager)`. The template is thread-safe once configured, so you can create it once and reuse it.

The main method is `execute`. It takes a `TransactionCallback<T>` and returns a value. For example, if you want to transfer money and return the new balance, you write `BigDecimal newBalance = txTemplate.execute(status -> { rajesh.debit(amount); priya.credit(amount); return rajesh.getBalance(); });`. The template begins a transaction, runs your lambda, and commits automatically when the lambda returns. If the lambda throws a `RuntimeException`, the template rolls back and re-throws.

When your code does not need to return anything, use `executeWithoutResult`. It takes a `Consumer<TransactionStatus>` instead of a function. For example `txTemplate.executeWithoutResult(status -> { rajesh.debit(amount); priya.credit(amount); });`. This is cleaner than `execute` with a `return null;` at the end. It was added in Spring 5.2 specifically so you do not have to return a dummy value.

The `TransactionStatus` object passed into the callback is powerful. You can call `status.setRollbackOnly()` to force a rollback without throwing an exception — useful when a business rule fails but you do not want to throw. For example `if (rajesh.getBalance().compareTo(amount) < 0) { status.setRollbackOnly(); return; }`.

You can configure the template just like the annotation attributes. `txTemplate.setPropagationBehavior(TransactionDefinition.PROPAGATION_REQUIRES_NEW)` sets propagation, `txTemplate.setIsolationLevel(TransactionDefinition.ISOLATION_READ_COMMITTED)` sets isolation, `txTemplate.setTimeout(5)` sets a five second timeout, and `txTemplate.setReadOnly(true)` marks it read-only.

Compared to `@Transactional`, the annotation is declarative and clean but it works through an AOP proxy, so it only applies when the method is called from outside the bean. `TransactionTemplate` is programmatic — the transaction boundary is the lambda, decided at runtime by actual method calls, so there is no proxy involved.

This is exactly why `TransactionTemplate` fixes the self-invocation problem. With `@Transactional`, if method `a()` in a bean calls `this.b()` where `b()` is annotated, the annotation on `b()` is ignored because the call does not go through the proxy — it is a plain `this` call. With `TransactionTemplate` there is no proxy, so you can start a transaction from any private helper method, even one called internally, and it always works. A senior developer reaches for `TransactionTemplate` when they need a transaction around a small block inside a larger method, or inside a method that is called internally, or when they need to react to the `TransactionStatus` mid-flight.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, there is a batch job that processes a list of pending transfers overnight. Each transfer must be its own independent transaction, because if transfer number three fails, transfers one and two should still be saved. If we put `@Transactional` on the whole batch method, one failure rolls back the entire batch. This is exactly what programmatic transaction management with `PROPAGATION_REQUIRES_NEW` solves — we wrap each single transfer in its own `TransactionTemplate.executeWithoutResult` call so each commits or rolls back on its own.

Problem 2 — The batch method and the single-transfer logic live in the same service class. The batch method calls the transfer method internally using `this`. If the transfer method relied on `@Transactional`, the annotation would be silently ignored because of self-invocation — the call never goes through the Spring proxy. This is exactly why we use `TransactionTemplate` inside the internal method: it starts a real transaction regardless of how the method was called.

Problem 3 — Sometimes a transfer should be quietly skipped when Rajesh does not have enough balance, without throwing a loud exception that pollutes the logs. This is exactly what `status.setRollbackOnly()` is for — we mark the transaction for rollback and return cleanly.

What the code will do. The `Account` class holds accountId, holderName, and balance with `debit` and `credit` methods. The `AccountRepository` loads and saves accounts. The `TransferService` holds a `TransactionTemplate` built from the injected `PlatformTransactionManager`. Its `runBatch` method loops over a list of transfers and calls the internal `transferOne` method for each. The `transferOne` method uses `executeWithoutResult` with `REQUIRES_NEW` so each transfer is its own transaction, uses `setRollbackOnly` when the balance is too low, and demonstrates that self-invocation still gets a real transaction. The demo wires everything, runs a batch of three transfers where the middle one fails, and shows that the other two still commit.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a batch of three transfers. Transfer one is SAV2001 to CUR3001 for Rs.50,000. Transfer two is CUR3001 to SAV2001 for Rs.9,999,999 which is far more than Priya's balance. Transfer three is SAV2001 to CUR3001 for Rs.25,000.

Step 1. The `runBatch` method starts. It is NOT inside any transaction yet. It loops and calls `transferOne` for the first request. This is a self-invocation using `this`.

Step 2. Inside `transferOne`, the `TransactionTemplate` begins a fresh REQUIRES_NEW transaction. Rajesh's balance is Rs.1,000,000 which is enough for Rs.50,000. The debit and credit happen, both accounts are saved, and the lambda returns normally, so the template commits. Rajesh is now at Rs.950,000 and Priya at Rs.300,000.

Step 3. The loop calls `transferOne` for the second request. A new transaction begins. Priya's balance is only Rs.300,000 which is less than Rs.9,999,999. The code calls `status.setRollbackOnly()` and returns. The template sees the rollback-only flag and rolls back. No exception is thrown, no money moves, and the loop continues normally.

Step 4. The loop calls `transferOne` for the third request. A new transaction begins. Rajesh has Rs.950,000 which is enough for Rs.25,000. The debit and credit happen and the template commits. Rajesh is now at Rs.925,000 and Priya at Rs.325,000.

Step 5. The batch finishes. Two transfers committed, one rolled back cleanly, and each was fully independent because of REQUIRES_NEW.

sections.s6_takeaway:
TransactionTemplate is Spring's way of doing programmatic transaction management. Instead of putting the Transactional annotation on a method and letting the AOP proxy start and end the transaction, I build a TransactionTemplate from the PlatformTransactionManager and wrap the code I want inside a callback. The template begins the transaction before my callback runs, commits it when the callback returns normally, and rolls it back if the callback throws a runtime exception. I use the execute method when I need to return a value, and executeWithoutResult when I do not, which avoids the ugly return null at the end.

In my banking project we had an overnight batch job that processed many pending transfers. We deliberately did not make the batch method transactional, because if one transfer failed we did not want to lose all the others. Instead, each single transfer ran inside its own TransactionTemplate call configured with REQUIRES_NEW propagation, so every transfer committed or rolled back completely independently. When Rajesh had insufficient balance we called setRollbackOnly on the TransactionStatus to roll back cleanly without throwing a loud exception.

The most important reason I reach for TransactionTemplate is the self-invocation problem. With the Transactional annotation, if a method in a bean calls another annotated method on the same bean using this, the annotation is silently ignored because the call never passes through the Spring proxy. Since TransactionTemplate is programmatic and does not rely on a proxy at all, I can start a real transaction from any internal helper method and it always works.

So the way I summarize it in an interview is that the annotation is declarative and clean for the common case, but TransactionTemplate gives me explicit, line-by-line control over the transaction boundary, lets me react to the transaction status mid-flight, makes each item in a batch independent, and sidesteps the self-invocation trap entirely. I choose it whenever I need a transaction around a small block, inside an internally-called method, or when the boundaries must be decided at runtime.

---

keyPoints: No proxy needed — works for self-invocation scenarios
Use when @Transactional proxy limitations are a problem
